title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
policy: Original book-faithful art; one distinct image per visible slot; no film character designs, green-skinned witch, or ruby shoes. Nine painted literary maps, including Kansas, replace the earlier diagram maps.

slots.name: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
slots.description: A Kansas cyclone sets Dorothy Gale down in a country of four coloured lands ringed by a desert nobody crosses. Walking a road of yellow brick to ask a wizard for a way home, she collects a scarecrow who wants brains, a tin man who wants a heart and a lion who wants courage — and finds that the wizard is a humbug, that the witch he sends her to kill is undone by a bucket of water, and that the shoes on her own feet could have taken her home on the first day.

slots.name: Dorothy Gale
slots.description: A plain-spoken Kansas girl who wants one thing throughout and keeps asking for it until somebody can give it to her.

slots.name: Toto
slots.description: Dorothy’s small black dog, who cannot talk, is frightened of very little, and twice changes the story by running at something.

slots.name: The Scarecrow
slots.description: A stuffed man two days old who believes he has no brains, and who solves most of the party’s problems anyway.

slots.name: The Tin Woodman
slots.description: A woodchopper rebuilt in tin joint by joint, who believes he cannot feel and is the gentlest of them.

slots.name: The Cowardly Lion
slots.description: A lion the size of a small horse who is afraid of everything and does the frightening thing regardless.

slots.name: Oz, the Great and Terrible
slots.description: The ruler of the Emerald City, who receives each visitor alone and in a different shape.

slots.name: The Wicked Witch of the West
slots.description: The one-eyed owner of the Winkie country, who commands wolves, crows and bees, and is afraid of water and the dark.

slots.name: The Good Witch of the North
slots.description: A small, wrinkled, cheerful witch of the northern country, whose protection travels with the person she gives it to.

slots.name: Glinda
slots.description: The Good Witch of the South, young to look at and the most powerful of the four, who trades help for the Golden Cap.

slots.name: The Wicked Witch of the East
slots.description: The owner of the Munchkin country and its people, who is under the farmhouse before the story properly begins.

slots.name: Aunt Em
slots.description: A farmer’s wife whom the sun and wind have worn thin and gray, and who still startles at a child laughing.

slots.name: Uncle Henry
slots.description: A gray, silent Kansas farmer who works from morning to night and reads the sky before anyone else does.

slots.name: Boq
slots.description: A rich Munchkin who keeps a house large enough for a party and reads a stranger’s clothes for what she must be.

slots.name: The Guardian of the Gates
slots.description: The green man who opens the city, fits every visitor with spectacles, and keeps the only key that unlocks them.

slots.name: The Soldier with the Green Whiskers
slots.description: The palace doorkeeper, who carries messages to a ruler he has never seen and is not allowed past the door.

slots.name: The Green Girl
slots.description: The palace maid who shows guests to their rooms, dresses Dorothy for her audience, and is kind about it.

slots.name: The Queen of the Field Mice
slots.description: The ruler of thousands of field mice, who pays a debt promptly and twice knows the way when nobody else does.

slots.name: The King of the Winged Monkeys
slots.description: The leader of a band bound by an old charm to obey whoever holds the Golden Cap, three times and no more.

slots.name: The Stork
slots.description: A long-necked bird with a nest of her own who stops mid-flight to pull something light out of a river.

slots.name: The China Princess
slots.description: A figure of painted china who can talk and move in her own country and would stiffen anywhere else.

slots.name: Mr Joker
slots.description: The clown of the china country, cracked in a hundred places from standing on his head once too often.

slots.name: The Silver Shoes
slots.description: The Wicked Witch of the East’s pointed silver shoes, which fit Dorothy exactly and carry a charm nobody in the East ever understood.

slots.name: The Golden Cap
slots.description: A cap circled with diamonds and rubies whose lining holds the words that summon the Winged Monkeys — three times to an owner, and no more.

slots.name: The Green Spectacles
slots.description: Locked green glasses issued at the city gate, worn night and day by everyone inside the walls.

slots.name: The Silk Heart
slots.description: A heart of silk stuffed with sawdust, fitted into a tin chest through a square cut in it and soldered over.

slots.name: The Bran-New Brains
slots.description: A measure of bran mixed with pins and needles, packed into a straw head and held in place with more straw.

slots.name: The Green Bottle of Courage
slots.description: A square green bottle poured into a carved green-gold dish, on the argument that courage is only courage once swallowed.

slots.name: The Silk Balloon
slots.description: Strips of light, dark and emerald green silk sewn into a bag over twenty feet long, glued airtight and hung with a clothes basket.

slots.name: The Witch of the North’s Slate
slots.description: A witch’s cap that becomes a slate when it is balanced on her nose and counted over, and writes its answer in chalk.

slots.name: The Oil-Can
slots.description: The can that keeps the Tin Woodman moving, carried in Dorothy’s basket after a year of rust taught him what happens without it.

slots.name: The Woodman’s Axe
slots.description: The axe that cost the Woodman his body piece by piece and that now clears trees, bridges, wildcats and wolves out of the party’s way.

slots.name: Dorothy’s Basket
slots.description: The covered basket she leaves Kansas with, which carries bread, then nuts, then fruit, then the oil-can.

slots.name: The Mouse Queen’s Whistle
slots.description: A little whistle given in thanks, worn round the neck, and worth a thousand mice whenever it is blown.

slots.name: Where the House Came Down
slots.description: A green Munchkin meadow of fruit trees and a brook, marked by the farmhouse that fell out of the sky onto it.

slots.name: Boq’s House
slots.description: The home of one of the richest Munchkins, whose lawn holds fiddlers, dancing and a loaded supper table.

slots.name: The Munchkin Cornfield
slots.description: A fenced field of ripe corn beside the road, with a pole in it holding a stuffed figure above the stalks.

slots.name: The Road Through the Forest
slots.description: Where the yellow bricks turn broken and uneven and the branches close overhead until the daylight goes.

slots.name: The Woodman’s Cottage
slots.description: A small hut of logs and branches in the trees, with a spring nearby and an oil-can on its shelf.

slots.name: Where the Lion Bounded Out
slots.description: A stretch of the road under thick branches where the growling of large animals carries out of the trees.

slots.name: The Camp Under the Great Tree
slots.description: A night stop in the forest, with a fire, a pile of chopped wood and a tree full of nuts nearby.

slots.name: The First Great Ditch
slots.description: A wide, steep-sided gulf full of jagged rocks that cuts the road and the forest clean across.

slots.name: The Second Ditch
slots.description: A gulf too broad to jump, in the part of the forest where the fiercest beasts of Oz are said to live.

slots.name: The Broad River
slots.description: A swift river between the dark forest and the bright country beyond it, crossed only by raft.

slots.name: The Deadly Poppy Field
slots.description: A great meadow of scarlet poppies whose scent puts anything made of flesh to sleep where it stands.

slots.name: The Field-Mouse Meadow
slots.description: Sweet grass and daisies past the poppies, thick with the burrows of a very numerous small people.

slots.name: The Green Farmhouse
slots.description: The first farm of the green country, where fences, clothes and skins have all taken the colour of the city ahead.

slots.name: The Emerald City
slots.description: The city at the exact centre of Oz, where the road of yellow brick ends at a wall and a studded gate.

slots.name: The Country of the West
slots.description: Rough, hilly, untilled ground with no road across it, watched from a long way off by its one-eyed owner.

slots.name: The Yellow Castle
slots.description: The Wicked Witch of the West’s castle, standing over the Winkie country that works for her.

slots.name: The Wood of the Fighting Trees
slots.description: The first rank of a southern wood, whose front trees take hold of anything that tries to walk in under them.

slots.name: The Dainty China Country
slots.description: A low white wall on the far side of the wood, with something very small and very brightly coloured behind it.

slots.name: The Bogs and Marshes
slots.description: Rank grass tall enough to hide the mud holes under it, on the way south out of the china country.

slots.name: The Great Forest
slots.description: An old wood of enormous trees and deep moss, whose animals are holding a meeting about a monster.

slots.name: The Hill of the Hammer-Heads
slots.description: A steep hillside of loose rock, with an armless people behind every boulder who will not let anyone across.

slots.name: The Quadling Farmhouse
slots.description: A red-painted farm among ripening grain and strong little bridges, kept by a woman who feeds strangers well.

slots.name: Glinda’s Castle
slots.description: A beautiful castle at the southern edge of the country, guarded at its gates by three girl soldiers.

slots.name: The Gale Farmhouse
slots.description: One small room, four walls and a roof, weathered gray by the same sun that has flattened the country around it.

slots.name: The Cyclone Cellar
slots.description: A dark hole dug under the floor, reached by a trap door and a ladder, for the days the wind comes.

slots.name: The Barnyard and Sheds
slots.description: Where the cows and horses are kept, and the first place a Kansas farmer goes when the sky turns.

slots.name: The Open Prairie
slots.description: Gray, cracked, treeless ground running flat to the edge of the sky in every direction.

slots.name: The New Farmhouse
slots.description: The house Uncle Henry builds where the old one stood, on the same bare stretch of prairie.

slots.name: The Great Gate
slots.description: The one way in: a gate thick with emeralds, with a bell beside it and a green man behind it.

slots.name: The Guardian’s Room
slots.description: A high arched room inside the gate, holding a great green box of spectacles and the only key that unlocks them.

slots.name: The Green Streets
slots.description: Marble pavements, green shops and green sweets, and people who pay for them with green pennies.

slots.name: The Palace of Oz
slots.description: The building in the middle of the city, guarded at its door by a soldier with a long green beard.

slots.name: The Launching Ground
slots.description: The open ground before the palace, where the whole city can gather to watch something rise.

slots.name: The Palace Gates
slots.description: The door the green-whiskered soldier keeps, and the mat every visitor is made to wipe their feet on.

slots.name: The Waiting Hall
slots.description: A green-carpeted room where the court assembles each morning to wait on a ruler none of them has seen.

slots.name: The Throne Room
slots.description: A great domed chamber of close-set emeralds, with one enormous light above and one green throne below.

slots.name: The Wizard’s Laboratory
slots.description: The tower room off the throne room where the Head, the costume, the beast and the ball of fire are kept when they are not frightening anybody.

slots.name: The Guest Corridor
slots.description: Seven passages and three flights of stairs up, where guests of the palace are given rooms and left.

slots.name: Dorothy’s Green Room
slots.description: A small bedroom with green silk sheets, a green fountain, a shelf of green books and a wardrobe that fits.

slots.name: The Front Doorstep
slots.description: The step outside the castle door, where anything the Winged Monkeys are carrying is set down.

slots.name: The Great Kitchen
slots.description: Pots, kettles, a swept floor and a wood fire, kept by whoever the Witch has most lately taken.

slots.name: The Iron-Fenced Yard
slots.description: A small yard behind a high iron fence, built to hold something that will not be harnessed.

slots.name: The Winkie Workshops
slots.description: The Winkies’ own quarter of the castle — their mess hall, their barracks rooms, and the benches where their tinsmiths do the work their owner sets them.

slots.name: The Cupboard Room
slots.description: Where the Witch keeps what is left of her power, on a shelf, behind a door she does not often open.

slots.name: The Watching Door
slots.description: The castle doorway the Witch sits in, where one eye does the work of a telescope over her whole country.

slots.name: The High China Wall
slots.description: A smooth white wall higher than a man, with no gate in it and nothing to climb but a made ladder.

slots.name: The Milkmaid’s Farm
slots.description: China barns and china fences, where a china cow is milked by a china girl until something startles it.

slots.name: The Princess’s Meadow
slots.description: Open china floor where the most beautifully dressed of the little people keeps a careful distance.

slots.name: Mr Joker’s Corner
slots.description: The pitch of the country’s clown, who has been mended so often that the cracks show all over him.

slots.name: The China Church
slots.description: A small painted church with a china steeple, standing near the low wall on the far side.

slots.name: The Low China Wall
slots.description: The shorter wall on the southern side, climbable from a lion’s back and easy to knock things off.

slots.name: The Castle Gates
slots.description: Gates kept by three young soldiers in red uniforms trimmed with gold, who take a name before anyone goes in.

slots.name: The Outer Court
slots.description: The court inside the gates, where visitors wait while their names are carried to the Witch of the South.

slots.name: The Tiring Room
slots.description: A room set aside for making oneself presentable: water, a comb, and space to be patted back into shape.

slots.name: The Ruby Throne Room
slots.description: A great room in which a throne cut from rubies stands, and the last unspent power in Oz is asked for.

slots.name: The Munchkins
slots.description: The blue people of the East, freed from the Wicked Witch of the East by a falling farmhouse.

slots.name: The Winkies
slots.description: The yellow people of the West, enslaved by the Witch through the Golden Cap and freed by a bucket of water.

slots.name: The Quadlings
slots.description: The red people of the South, short, chubby and good-natured, who keep their roads paved and their bridges strong.

slots.name: The Winged Monkeys
slots.description: A free forest people bound by an old sentence to obey the owner of the Golden Cap three times over.

slots.name: The Field Mice
slots.description: Thousands of mice under one queen, who pay a debt with string, a truck and directions.

slots.name: The Hammer-Heads
slots.description: An armless people who own a hill and defend it with their heads, and let nobody over it on foot.

slots.name: The China People
slots.description: Milkmaids, princesses, clowns and livestock, all of painted china, all breakable, all content where they are.

slots.name: The Beasts of the Great Forest
slots.description: Tigers, elephants, bears and wolves who hold meetings, and who will crown anyone who removes their monster.

slots.name: The Four Countries and Their Colours
slots.description: Oz is divided into four countries around a green city at the exact centre. The East belongs to the Munchkins and is blue; the West to the Winkies and is yellow; the South to the Quadlings and is red; the North is the home of the good witch who meets Dorothy. Each country keeps its colour in its fences, houses, clothes and crops, so a traveller always knows which quarter they are standing in.

slots.name: The Deadly Desert
slots.description: A desert surrounds Oz on all four sides and nobody crosses it. It is the reason a girl who wants to go home cannot simply walk, the reason the Winged Monkeys refuse a direct order, and the reason the only two people known to have arrived here came through the air.

slots.name: Four Witches and One Wizard
slots.description: There were four witches in Oz: the North and South good, the East and West wicked. Their power is uneven — the Witch of the North says plainly that she was not strong enough to free the Munchkins herself. The Wizard in the Emerald City is spoken of as more powerful than all of them together, though nobody consulted has ever seen him.

slots.name: The Charm of the Golden Cap
slots.description: Whoever owns the Golden Cap may command the Winged Monkeys three times, and no more. The charm is written inside the lining and worked by standing on the left foot, then the right, then both, saying the words in order. Ownership passes with the Cap itself, and the count belongs to the owner, not to the Cap.

slots.name: The Green Spectacles
slots.description: Every visitor to the Emerald City is fitted at the gate with green spectacles, locked on with golden bands. The Guardian of the Gates keeps the only key and the rule is said to date from the building of the city.

slots.name: The Silver Shoes
slots.description: The Wicked Witch of the East was proud of these shoes and the Munchkins knew there was a charm on them without ever learning what it was. They fit Dorothy exactly, cannot be worn out by walking, and are feared by at least one witch who understands what they can do.

slots.name: How This Chronology Was Reconstructed
slots.description: The novel dates nothing and names no season, so the calendar in this world is editorial. Day one is fixed at 1 August only so that ripe corn and blooming poppies sit in a plausible month; the year is arbitrary. Every interval between scenes, however, is the book’s own: the nights on the road, the three days and four nights the tinsmiths work, the three days of waiting after the Witch dies, the three days of sewing silk, and the several days lost in the yellow fields are all counted from the text. Read the day numbers as elapsed time, not as dates.

slots.name: The Text Behind This World
slots.description: The manuscript follows the complete public-domain text of L. Frank Baum’s novel in Project Gutenberg eBook #55, including Baum’s own Introduction. Every narrative paragraph from Chapters I–XXIV is assigned once in source order; Gutenberg packaging and illustration placeholders are excluded. Summaries, event divisions, chronology, maps and state notes are editorial.

slots.name: The Pictures in This World
slots.description: Every portrait, item and place picture is one of W. W. Denslow’s illustrations for the 1900 first edition, which are in the public domain. The files come from Wikimedia Commons, were checked one by one against the entity they are attached to, and are shipped with the book rather than linked to another site. A few entities are deliberately left without a picture where no illustration of them exists: the Wicked Witch of the East, who is dead before the story opens, is one.

slots.name: The Maps in This World
slots.description: Baum published no map of Oz with the 1900 edition, so every layer here is an interpretation. Six of the seven — the Land of Oz, the Emerald City, the Palace, the Yellow Castle, the China Country and Glinda’s Castle — are AI-generated maps supplied by this world’s author; the Kansas layer was drawn for this world from what the text states. The six carry names and country the 1900 book does not: the Land of Oz puts the poppy field and the china country where the sequels put them rather than where Dorothy meets them on the road, and its border figures follow the 1939 film’s designs; the palace plans name Princess Ozma and the Book of Records, which arrive in later books; the city is given four

maps.name: The Yellow Castle of the West
